item.title: Asuka-nabe: The Ancient Milk Hot Pot of Asuka — Guide
item.description: Asuka-nabe is one of Japan’s most unusual regional hot pots: a chicken-and-vegetable nabe simmered in a broth enriched with milk, giving it a mellow, creamy character unlike any other Japanese pot. Its origins are traced to the Asuka period over 1,300 years ago, when dairy foods and cattle-keeping were introduced to Japan from the Asian mainland via the imperial court based in Asuka — making this humble dish a living echo of Japan’s very first encounter with milk.

item.title: A Nagoya Meshi Food Tour: Eating Through Japan's Boldest Food City — Guide
item.description: No Japanese city guards a food identity as fiercely as Nagoya, whose ‘Nagoya meshi’ canon — eel hitsumabushi, miso-sauced katsu, peppery tebasaki wings, clay-pot miso nikomi udon, morning ogura toast and more — grew from the region’s dark hatcho miso and tamari brewing traditions into a cuisine found nowhere else. Eating through it is the city’s best itinerary: a self-guided day can run from kissaten breakfast through a noodle lunch to an izakaya wing crawl, while guided evening food tours thread the lantern-lit alleys and counter bars with a local who knows which queue is worth it.

item.title: Hitsumabushi: Nagoya's Three-Way Eel Feast — Guide
item.description: Hitsumabushi is the flagship of ‘Nagoya meshi’, the city’s proudly idiosyncratic food culture, and it turns grilled eel into a ritual of three acts: finely sliced, crisp-grilled unagi arrives on rice in a lacquered wooden tub, and you eat the first quarter plain, the second with wasabi, spring onion and shredded nori, and the third drowned in hot dashi as a fragrant ochazuke — before finishing with a fourth portion in whichever style won.

item.title: Omi Chanpon: Hikone's Gentle Noodle Soul Food — Guide
item.description: Omi chanpon is Shiga’s homegrown noodle dish, born at a Hikone noodle shop in the 1960s and now the prefecture’s definitive everyday comfort food. Unlike its rich, pork-boned Nagasaki namesake, the Omi version rests on a delicate golden broth of kombu and bonito — closer to refined udon dashi — over which a mountain of stir-steamed cabbage, bean sprouts, onions and pork is piled onto springy medium noodles, and the local ritual is to douse the last third with a swirl of vinegar, which brightens the whole bowl.

item.title: Obanzai Guide: Kyoto's Home-Style Comfort Cooking
item.description: If kaiseki is Kyoto’s formal art, obanzai is its soul food: the everyday home cooking of Kyoto households, built on local seasonal vegetables, simple techniques, frugality, and quiet good taste. Obanzai is what Kyoto people actually eat at home — small dishes of simmered vegetables, tofu, beans, dried fish, and pickles, made to use ingredients fully and waste nothing. For visitors tired of heavy or touristy food, an obanzai meal is a revelation: gentle, healthy, deeply satisfying, and authentically Kyoto.

item.title: Okinawa Soba Guide: What It Is, Where to Eat & Types
item.description: Despite the name, Okinawa soba contains no buckwheat — it’s a beloved local comfort food of thick, chewy wheat noodles in a clear, savoury pork-and-bonito broth, topped with tender pork, fish cake, pickled ginger and spring onion. Found everywhere from humble shokudo (diners) to dedicated specialists, it’s one of the first tastes of Okinawa most visitors fall for. Regional variations and toppings — from meaty soki to braised rafute — make it endlessly satisfying.
